segments.t: Near the entrance, Thorsten spots a familiar visitor and breathes a huge sigh of relief: boss Sabine stayed away and sent her assistant Beyza instead. Thorsten immediately vows to the camera that today is the day he asks Beyza out, though Beyza is strictly here on business. Listen to the German exchange first.
Gott sei Dank ist Sabine heute nicht da!
Das ist Beyza, die Assistentin von Sabine.
Heute frage ich sie nach einem Abendessen.
Hallo Beyza! Schön, dass du hier bist.
Hallo Thorsten! Sabine kommt heute leider nicht.
Kein Problem! Möchtest du zuerst einen Kaffee trinken?
Nein danke, ich habe heute leider nicht viel Zeit.
Und, wollen wir direkt ins Büro gehen?
Let's unpack Thorsten's relieved reaction, how he introduces Beyza, and how they head into the meeting.
Gott sei Dank ist Sabine heute nicht da!

'Thank goodness Sabine is not here today!' Word for word, the opening exclamation says 'to God be thanks', the everyday German twin of 'thank goodness!' Because that whole exclamation fills the first slot, 'is' steps straight into second position right behind it.
Das ist Beyza, die Assistentin von Sabine.

'That is Beyza, Sabine's assistant.' Rather than adding an apostrophe-'s' to a name the way English does, everyday spoken German links people with the word for 'of' or 'from' — literally 'the assistant of Sabine', complete with the feminine job ending.
Heute frage ich sie nach einem Abendessen.

'Today I am going to ask her to dinner.' Notice how German needs no special future helper when a time word like 'today' already makes the plan clear: 'today ask I her' does the whole job, ending with the compound word for 'evening meal'.
Hallo Beyza! Schön, dass du hier bist.

'Hello Beyza! Nice that you're here.' This warm greeting — literally 'nice that you here are' — is one of the friendliest ways to welcome a guest or coworker. Notice how the word for 'that' sends 'are' right to the end of the clause.
Hallo Thorsten! Sabine kommt heute leider nicht.

'Hello Thorsten! Unfortunately, Sabine is not coming today.' Slipping the single word for 'unfortunately' into the middle of a sentence softens bad news or a change of plans without needing a whole extra clause.
Kein Problem! Möchtest du zuerst einen Kaffee trinken?

'No problem! Would you like to drink a coffee first?' Pairing 'no' with 'problem' works just like in English, followed by a polite phrase for 'would you like to...?' that sends the word for 'drink' cleanly to the end.
Und, wollen wir direkt ins Büro gehen?

'So, shall we go straight to the office?' Beyza uses the contraction for 'into the office' — squeezing two little words into one neat syllable — and rounds off with 'shall we?' to get straight down to work. Now let's hear the whole arrival scene once more.
Gott sei Dank ist Sabine heute nicht da!
Das ist Beyza, die Assistentin von Sabine.
Heute frage ich sie nach einem Abendessen.
Hallo Beyza! Schön, dass du hier bist.
Hallo Thorsten! Sabine kommt heute leider nicht.
Kein Problem! Möchtest du zuerst einen Kaffee trinken?
Nein danke, ich habe heute leider nicht viel Zeit.
Und, wollen wir direkt ins Büro gehen?

Beyza skips the small talk and leads a nervous Thorsten straight toward the office to inspect the numbers. You have heard how to say 'thank goodness', introduce an assistant, say you don't have much time, and suggest heading into the office. See you next time!
Bis später!
